Visual essay · reproduction and extension

When does a self-predicting network get simpler?

On MNIST, self-modeling narrows the classifier. On CIFAR, the ordering inverts. On IMDB, the effect disappears. A toy dial shows the scale cheat behind one failure. A slowed self-model head shows the other is a mechanism that dies before it acts.

v1 · guided cut 17 min Updated 2026-10-19 Premakumar et al., 2024
The paradox The mechanism The stop-gradient The skip test The pressure The scoreboard What next

How to read this. This is the guided cut: the argument, the mechanism, and the one experiment that changes the interpretation. The lab notebook has every panel, probe, and RLCT detail. Read this for the argument; open the lab for the evidence.

data.text/markdown:
The paradox

The paper's claim is simple. Add a self-prediction term to the loss, and the network gets simpler: the classifier weights narrow, a formal complexity measure falls, and test accuracy barely moves. We reproduced it on MNIST. The same recipe fails, in different ways, on CIFAR-10 and IMDB.

data.text/html:
MNIST · Figure 2A
0.0974 → 0.0812
Narrower weights with more self-modeling. The paper's effect, reproduced within 0.001.
CIFAR-10 · Figure 3A
0.0252 → 0.0292
The ordering inverts: the baseline is the narrowest curve. Accuracy still matches.
IMDB · Figure 4A
0.232 flat
No separation across AW, and about 9x below the paper's 2.05. Accuracy matches at 85.2%.

data.text/markdown: Figure 1. Three panels, three verdicts. MNIST and CIFAR numbers are the epoch-50 classifier weight SD; IMDB is the weight SD at the end of training. Sources: mnist_detach_ablation.json, cifar_fig3_probes.json, imdb_fig4.json.

One number does not explain all three. The rest of the essay is the search for what does. Two candidates survive. First, the self-model loss can be gamed: if the target moves, the cheapest way to reduce the error is to shrink the thing being predicted. Second, the pressure can die before it acts. On IMDB the self-model gradient share falls to about 2% by epoch 20, while MNIST stays at 14% to 18%.

The mechanism

A hidden layer produces a cloud of activations. A classifier reads the cloud. A self-model head tries to predict it from the same hidden layer. The self-model term is happy when the cloud is easy to predict. The cheapest way to make it easy is to shrink the cloud. The classifier then grows to keep the logits fixed.

At AW = 5, the detached run has hidden norm 2.92 and classifier norm 5.07. Without the stop-gradient: 2.30 and 6.88. The self-model error is 0.000 in both modes. Both solve the prediction task; only the detached run keeps the representation at its natural scale.

Figure 2. The compression dial. The hidden cloud is a 2D toy trained for each AW; the dial interpolates 11 precomputed frames. Both modes reach self-model error 0.000. Drag the dial, click the norm strip, press Play, or toggle the stop-gradient. Source: compression_dial.json; generator: scripts/build_compression_dial.py.

The stop-gradient

The self-model target is a.detach(). It looks like an implementation detail. It is the hinge. Before you look: which dataset is sensitive to dropping it?
Reveal to see the ablation.

The skip test

Our first CIFAR run used a standard ResNet-18. The paper says the input to the hidden layer includes the output of block 4 and the skip connections from block 3. That is the largest architectural difference between our run and the paper's. We implemented the simplest faithful version: global-pool block 3 and block 4, concatenate the 256- and 512-vectors, and feed the 768-vector into the 2000-wide hidden layer. The self-model target is the concatenation of that input and the hidden activations.

Figure 5. The block-3 skip lowers the level but not the ordering. Lines are means over two seeds; bands are 95% CIs. At 150 epochs, batch 512. The paper reports the opposite ordering: the baseline is widest and self-modeling narrows it. The batch-64 probe is in Table 1. Source: cifar_skip.json; script: scripts/cifar_skip_experiment.py.Table 1. The batch-64 probe. One seed, 75 epochs. At the paper's batch size the absolute SD is higher, but the ordering is still inverted. Source: cifar_skip.json.
model AW 0 AW 2 accuracy

spatial 0.1050 0.1101 0.917

data.text/markdown: The skip changes the level, not the ordering. At 150 epochs the standard model goes from 0.0400 at AW 0 to 0.0508 at AW 2. The block-3 model goes from 0.0321 to 0.0402. The skip lowers the absolute SD, but the self-modeling run is still wider. We also ran the paper's batch size. At batch 64 we used a spatial skip: concatenate block 3 with an upsampled block 4, fuse them with a 1x1 convolution to 512, then pool. At 75 epochs, the standard model goes from 0.0759 to 0.1001; the spatial skip goes from 0.1050 to 0.1101. The absolute SD is much higher, and the ordering is still inverted. The block-3 intervals do not overlap. The standard run's two-seed intervals do, so read that arm as a sign rather than a measurement. The batch-64 probe is one seed. The paper uses 150 epochs and does not pin down the skip placement. Both skip placements fail to flip the ordering. This is a negative result for the obvious architectural fix, not a proof that no implementation would work.

data.text/html: The stop-gradient is essential to the MNIST mechanism and irrelevant to the CIFAR inversion. Both can be true.

data.text/markdown:
The pressure has to persist

On IMDB the MNIST effect was missing. The identity diagnostics show why: the self-model head learns a shortcut early, and the self-model share of the hidden-layer gradient falls to about 2% by epoch 20. On MNIST the share stays at 14% to 18% at epoch 50. If that is the mechanism, slowing the head down should bring the effect back. We scaled the self-model rows' gradient by 0.01 and 0.001 and re-ran IMDB at AW 0, 100, and 500.

The slowed-head control is causal evidence for the identity mechanism, with caveats: three seeds, 100 epochs, accuracy drops, and the effect is not monotone in AW. It explains our missing IMDB effect. It does not reproduce the paper's IMDB numbers.
Two failures, two mechanisms. Build the figure one piece at a time, or show both.

data.text/html:
CIFAR-10 · units

SD / |W| stays flat. The activations shrink and the classifier grows to keep the logits fixed. The wider SD is a units change, not a new complexity.

IMDB · timing

The pressure dies. The self-model share of the hidden-layer gradient falls to about 2% by epoch 20. Slow the head down and the effect comes back.

data.text/markdown: Figure 7. Two failures, two mechanisms. CIFAR's inversion is a units change: the classifier norm grows with the SD, so SD/|W| is flat, and the block-3 skip does not change the ordering. IMDB's null is a timing problem: the self-model gradient share falls to about 2% by epoch 20. Sources: cifar_fig3_probes.json, identity_diagnostics.json, slowhead_control.json.

data.text/markdown: Table 2. Replication matrix. Yes means the paper's ordering and scale are within our interval; No means the ordering is inverted or the effect is missing; Partly means accuracy matches but the effect does not. 3A was also tested with pooled and spatial skips, at batch 512 and 64; the ordering stayed inverted. Full notes and probes are in the lab notebook.

What next

Three experiments would change the conclusion:
  • A 10-seed batch-64 protocol. Our batch-64 probe is one seed and 75 epochs. The paper uses 150 epochs. A 10-seed run at the paper's exact batch, schedule, and augmentation is the remaining faithful CIFAR test.
  • More seeds for the slow-head control. Three seeds and 100 epochs is a sign. Ten seeds and 250 epochs is a measurement.
  • A rank diagnostic for IMDB. The hidden layer is 128 units from a 64-dimensional embedding. A rank test would show whether the self-model rows learn a projection, as the weight distance suggests.
The effect is real, fragile, and conditional. That is a more useful result than a clean reproduction. A reproduction that only reports the panels it matches would have missed both mechanisms.
